title: Streaming Responses
subtitle: Server-sent events, real-time display, and latency
author: KERNAL Team

whyItExists.problem: LLMs generate tokens one at a time. Without streaming, the API buffers the entire response before returning — users wait 10-30 seconds staring at a blank screen for long generations.
whyItExists.solution: Streaming (Server-Sent Events / SSE) sends each token to the client as soon as it is generated. Users see output immediately and can read while the model generates the rest.
whyItExists.whenToUse: Any user-facing chat UI, any response over ~200 tokens. Users tolerate 'watching it write' much better than waiting.
whyItExists.whenNotToUse: Batch processing where you need the complete output before continuing. JSON extraction where partial JSON is unusable.

explainModes.beginner: Without streaming, you wait 15 seconds then get all the text at once. With streaming, text appears word by word immediately — just like watching someone type. It feels much faster even if the total time is the same.
explainModes.simple: Streaming uses Server-Sent Events (SSE): the server sends a continuous stream of data chunks to the client. Each chunk contains one or a few tokens. Your app displays each chunk as it arrives, creating the 'typing' effect.
explainModes.standard: Streaming uses HTTP chunked transfer encoding with the SSE protocol. The server sends event: content_block_delta events with delta.text payloads. The client accumulates these to build the full response. The connection stays open until the model finishes.
explainModes.technical: The Anthropic SDK's stream() method returns an async context manager that yields MessageStreamEvent objects. The final message (stream.get_final_message()) includes complete usage stats. For React/Next.js, the Vercel AI SDK wraps LLM streaming into a ReadableStream compatible with the web Response API.
explainModes.deepDive: SSE events over HTTP/2 multiplexing allow streaming alongside other requests on the same connection. For LLM proxies (like LiteLLM), all provider streaming is normalized to OpenAI's format: data: {choices:[{delta:{content:'...'}}]} events. Time-to-first-token (TTFT) is the key latency metric for streaming UX — it's the prefill time before generation starts.

content.text: By default, the API waits until the full response is generated before returning. Streaming sends tokens as they are generated, dramatically improving perceived latency. Users start reading immediately instead of waiting for the full response.

content.code:
import anthropic
client = anthropic.Anthropic()

# Streaming with the Anthropic SDK
with client.messages.stream(
    model="claude-sonnet-5-5",
    max_tokens=1024,
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "Tell me a short story about a robot learning to paint."}]
) as stream:
    for text in stream.text_stream:
        print(text, end="", flush=True)  # Prints each token as it arrives

# Get final message with usage stats
final = stream.get_final_message()
print(f"\n\nTokens: in={final.usage.input_tokens}, out={final.usage.output_tokens}")

content.text: Streaming to a Next.js / Web API Response
For user-facing chat UIs, always use streaming. The perceived latency improvement is dramatic — users rate streamed responses as 'faster' even when total generation time is identical.
Don't try to parse JSON from a streaming response mid-stream. Buffer the full text and parse after stream.get_final_message(). Partial JSON will throw parse errors.

questions.question: What is the primary benefit of streaming LLM responses?
options: Users see output immediately as tokens arrive, improving perceived performance
questions.explanation: Streaming makes the app feel instant because the user reads output as it's generated rather than waiting 10-30 seconds for the full response.

questions.question: Which protocol do LLM APIs use for streaming?
questions.explanation: LLM streaming uses SSE (Server-Sent Events) — a unidirectional, text-based HTTP streaming protocol. The server sends event: data: lines over a persistent HTTP connection.

questions.question: When should you NOT use streaming?
options: Batch processing where you need complete JSON before proceeding
questions.explanation: Streaming sends partial text. If your code needs to parse the full JSON output, process it in a database, or chain it to another step, wait for the complete response — partial JSON will throw errors.

faq.q: Can I cancel a streaming request mid-way?
faq.a: Yes. Break out of the for loop or call stream.close() to cancel. The API stops generating and you're only charged for tokens generated up to that point.

The delay between sending the request and receiving the first token. This is the 'prefill' time — the model processes your input before starting generation. For long prompts, TTFT can be 2-5 seconds even with streaming.

faq.q: How do I stream to multiple clients simultaneously?
faq.a: Make separate API calls per client. You can't broadcast one LLM stream to multiple subscribers directly — but you can store the full response as it streams and use a pub/sub system (Redis, SSE broadcast) to fan it out.
